name: boeing_docket_chronology
document:
# A chronology of United States v. The Boeing Company, every event quoted from its page

## The question

What happened in the criminal case over Boeing's deception of the FAA about the 737 MAX, in
what order, who said what, and which facts did one side assert and another deny? Every entry
must point at the words on a filing's page that state it.

## The corpus

14 filings from the docket of United States v. The Boeing Company, N.D. Tex. No.
4:21-cr-00005 (CourtListener docket 29089563), as CourtListener's RECAP archive holds them:
ECF 4, 52, 58, 116, 185, 197, 221-1, 233, 245, 282, 312, 312-1, 334 and 358. They run from the January 2021
deferred prosecution agreement, through the crash victims' families' motions under the Crime
Victims' Rights Act and the court's opinions on them, the 2024 plea agreement and the
order rejecting it, to the 2025 non-prosecution agreement and the order granting the
government's motion to dismiss. Hearing transcripts are left out. `app/seeds/data/boeing/SOURCES.md` lists each
file's address, hash and fetch time.

A filing that is not among these 14 is outside what this chronology can see.

## Step 1 - read every page

Each filing is read page by page from its PDF's text layer. Each page keeps the filing's ECF
number, attachment number, filing date and docket description.

## Step 2 - list the events on each page

A model reads one page at a time and lists up to three events it states: something that
happened, or a position the court or a party takes. For each it writes one sentence and
copies the words that state it. It is not shown any other page.

## Step 3 - date each event, and name its speaker and topic

A model reads each event beside its page and gives the day it happened, how precisely the
page states that day, whose act or assertion it is (court, government, Boeing, the families,
or other), and one of eleven topics. A filing's own act, such as a ruling or an argument,
takes the day it was filed. An event whose page gives no date is dropped.

## Step 4 - pin each event to its words

A model copies the words on the page that state the event. The runtime finds them on the
page, exactly, and records where they sit; a quote it cannot find is sent back to the model.
An event no words on its page state is dropped.

## Step 5 - one row per event, in date order

Where a later filing quotes an earlier one word for word, with the same date, speaker and
topic, the earlier filing's copy is kept. The events are then put in date order, and in
docket order within a day. Events stated in different words stay separate rows.

## Step 6 - find the disputed facts

A model reads every event on each topic and says whether one side asserts a fact another
denies, with the strongest quote for each side, picked from the topic's own quotes. Every
topic it marks disputed goes to a reviewer, who reads both quotes and settles the summary.

## The results

The chronology: every dated, quoted event, in order, with its pin cite. The disputes: each
topic's status as the reviewer left it, with the quotes on each side. A report lists both,
each quote linked to its page. The filings come from CourtListener's RECAP archive, run by
Free Law Project; the reading of them is this workflow's, not Free Law Project's.

llm.prompt_instructions:
You are reading one page of a filing in United States v. The Boeing Company (N.D. Tex. No. 4:21-cr-00005), the criminal case over Boeing's deception of the FAA about the 737 MAX. The page is one of about 480 across 14 filings, which run from the January 2021 deferred prosecution agreement, through the crash victims' families' fight under the Crime Victims' Rights Act (CVRA), the 2024 plea agreement and the court's rejection of it, to the 2025 non-prosecution agreement and dismissal. A newsroom is building a chronology of the case in which every entry is pinned to the words on a page.

Your job is to list the events on this page that belong on a timeline of the case. An event is one of two things:
- something that happened: a crash, a meeting, a communication, a payment, a filing, a hearing, an agreement being entered, an order or ruling, a determination, an admission;
- a position the court or a party takes on a question the case turns on: a holding or finding, an argument, an objection, a request for relief.

The terms of an agreement or an order are not events one by one. Its being entered is one event, and a headline term such as a penalty, a payment, a length of years or a monitor may be one more; its procedures, definitions, cooperation duties and boilerplate are not events. Leave out the caption, headers and footers, tables of contents, signature blocks and certificates of service; statements of law that are not about this case; background the page recounts only in passing; and anything mentioned only as a citation. List at most three events, the ones a reader of the case's history most needs. Many pages hold one or two, and many hold none: return an empty list for those.

For each event give:
1. "statement": one sentence in your own words saying who did or asserted what, and when if the page says when. Name the actor: the Court, the government, Boeing, the families, or whoever it is.
2. "quote": the words on this page that state the event, copied exactly. Keep the same spelling, capitals, punctuation and quotation marks, and any odd space the PDF's text layer put inside a word or before a comma. Keep it to one or two sentences, and never join words across a footnote, a page header or a line you skipped.

What becomes of your list: each event becomes a row of its own. Another step dates it and names its speaker and topic. A third finds your quote on this page and pins the event to it; an event whose words it cannot find there is dropped. A reviewer reads each event beside its quote, highlighted on the page. You are not shown the other pages, or what anything else in the case says.

Worked example. Part of page 8 of ECF No. 58, the government's response to the families' motions:
"A. Boeing’s Illegal Conduct
On October 29, 2018, Lion Air Flight 610 took off from Jakarta, Indonesia , and, shortly
after takeoff, crashed into the Java Sea.  SOF ¶ 48.  None of the 189 crewmembers and passengers
survived.  Id.  Similarly, on March 10, 2019, Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 departed Addis Ababa,
Ethiopia, and, shortly after takeoff, crashed.  Id.  ¶ 53."
→
{"events": [
  {"statement": "Lion Air Flight 610 crashed into the Java Sea shortly after taking off from Jakarta on October 29, 2018.",
   "quote": "On October 29, 2018, Lion Air Flight 610 took off from Jakarta, Indonesia , and, shortly after takeoff, crashed into the Java Sea."},
  {"statement": "Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 crashed shortly after taking off from Addis Ababa on March 10, 2019.",
   "quote": "on March 10, 2019, Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 departed Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and, shortly after takeoff, crashed."}
]}
The quotes keep the page's stray space before a comma, and leave out the citations "SOF ¶ 48" and "Id."

llm.prompt_instructions:
You are dating and labelling one event in United States v. The Boeing Company (N.D. Tex. No. 4:21-cr-00005), the criminal case over Boeing's deception of the FAA about the 737 MAX. An earlier step read one page of a filing and listed the events it states; this is one of them, with the words it copied from the page. Your answer places the event in a public chronology of the case, lets a reader filter it by who acted and by topic, and groups it with the other events on its topic, where a later step looks for facts one side asserts and another denies. An event you leave undated is dropped from the chronology. A reviewer sees your date, speaker and topic beside the quote. You are shown this one page and nothing else from the case.

Return:
1. "date": the day the event happened, as YYYY-MM-DD.
   - Where the page says when it happened ("On January 7, 2021, ...", "in March 2019"), that date. For a month or a year alone, give its first day.
   - Where the event is this filing's own act (the Court holds, finds, orders or rejects in this order; a party argues, moves or objects in this brief), the day the filing was filed, which you are given.
   - Otherwise null: the page reports something done elsewhere and does not say when. Never work a date out from what you know about the case beyond this page.
2. "date_precision": "day", "month" or "year" for how much of the date the page or the filing date states; "none" where date is null.
3. "speaker": whose act or assertion the event is.
   - "court": the district court or the court of appeals.
   - "government": the Department of Justice, its prosecutors, the United States.
   - "boeing": The Boeing Company or its lawyers.
   - "families": the crash victims' families, their representatives and their lawyers.
   - "other": anyone else, such as the FAA, an airline, an amicus or an expert.
   Where an order reports a party's argument, the speaker is that party. Where the page reports a happening no party performed, such as a crash, the speaker is whoever filed the page, since the event is their account. In a document both parties signed (the deferred prosecution, plea and non-prosecution agreements), the speaker is "government" unless the words are Boeing's own admission or undertaking.
4. "topic": the one of these the event is most about, written exactly as named:
   - "crashes": the Lion Air Flight 610 and Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 crashes and the 346 people who died
   - "fraud_offense": what Boeing did to deceive the FAA about the 737 MAX (MCAS, the Aircraft Evaluation Group), the conspiracy charge, and what Boeing admitted
   - "dpa_terms": the January 2021 deferred prosecution agreement: its terms, payments and obligations, and how it was negotiated
   - "crime_victim_status": whether the crash victims' families are 'crime victims' under the Crime Victims' Rights Act, including whether Boeing's crime directly and proximately caused the deaths
   - "victims_rights_violation": whether the government violated the families' CVRA rights, such as the right to confer, before it reached the agreement
   - "remedy": what the court can or should do about a CVRA violation: rescinding the agreement, arraignment, conditions, supervisory power
   - "dpa_breach": the 2024 determination that Boeing breached the deferred prosecution agreement
   - "plea_agreement": the 2024 plea agreement: the guilty plea, fine, probation, and whether the court should accept it
   - "independent_monitor": the independent compliance monitor: who selects it, who it reports to, and the diversity and inclusion provision
   - "npa_and_dismissal": the 2025 non-prosecution agreement and the government's motion to dismiss the case
   - "case_procedure": hearings, schedules, appeals, mandamus petitions and other steps in how the case was run

Worked example. ECF No. 58, filed 2022-02-08, the government's response to the families' motions. Event: "The government argues the families are not crime victims under the CVRA." Words from the page: "nor is such relief warranted in any event  because the Movants are not “crime victims” under the CVRA." →
{"date": "2022-02-08", "date_precision": "day", "speaker": "government", "topic": "crime_victim_status"}
The argument is this brief's own act, so it takes the day the brief was filed.

A second event on page 8 of the same filing: "Lion Air Flight 610 crashed into the Java Sea shortly after taking off from Jakarta on October 29, 2018." →
{"date": "2018-10-29", "date_precision": "day", "speaker": "government", "topic": "crashes"}
The page states the day, and the government is the one giving this account.

llm.prompt_instructions:
You are pinning one event in United States v. The Boeing Company (N.D. Tex. No. 4:21-cr-00005) to the words on its page that state it. An earlier step read the page, wrote the event as a sentence, and copied the words it took to state it; those words may be slightly off. The runtime looks for your quote in the page text below and pins the event there. A reader of the case's chronology clicks the event and sees your quote highlighted on the page, so the quote has to say what the event says. You are shown this one page and nothing else from the case.

Return "span" as {"quote": ..., "prefix": ..., "suffix": ...}:
- "quote": the words that state the event, copied exactly from the page text. Take the earlier step's words where the page holds them as written. Otherwise copy the shortest run of words that states the event: one or two sentences, never joined across a footnote or a page header. Keep the page's spelling, capitals, punctuation and quotation marks, and any odd space the PDF's text layer put inside a word or before a comma. Line breaks may be written as spaces.
- "prefix" and "suffix": leave them out, unless the same words appear more than once on the page. Then copy a few words from just before the quote as "prefix", or just after it as "suffix", so they point to one place.

Where no words on the page state the event, return "span": null. The event is then dropped from the chronology rather than pinned to words that do not say it.

Worked example. Event: "Lion Air Flight 610 crashed into the Java Sea shortly after taking off from Jakarta on October 29, 2018." Earlier step's words: "On October 29, 2018, Lion Air Flight 610 took off from Jakarta, Indonesia, and shortly after takeoff crashed into the Java Sea." The page reads:
"On October 29, 2018, Lion Air Flight 610 took off from Jakarta, Indonesia , and, shortly
after takeoff, crashed into the Java Sea."
The earlier step dropped a space and two commas, so copy the page:
{"span": {"quote": "On October 29, 2018, Lion Air Flight 610 took off from Jakarta, Indonesia , and, shortly after takeoff, crashed into the Java Sea."}}

llm.prompt_instructions:
You are reading every dated event on one topic in United States v. The Boeing Company (N.D. Tex. No. 4:21-cr-00005), the criminal case over Boeing's deception of the FAA about the 737 MAX, to find a fact one side asserts and another denies. A newsroom publishes, for each topic, whether its fact is disputed, a short summary, and the strongest quote on each side. A person reviews every topic you mark disputed, with your two quotes side by side, before it is published; a topic you mark undisputed is published without that review. You are shown this topic's events and nothing else from the case.

The events come as lists in date order: item i of the dates, speakers, statements, pin cites and quotes is one event.

A dispute is a fact, finding or legal conclusion that one speaker asserts and another speaker denies or contests. One speaker changing its position over time is not a dispute between sides, and two speakers describing different parts of the topic do not dispute each other.

Return:
1. "disputed": true where the events hold such a pair; false otherwise.
2. "summary": one or two sentences. Where disputed, name the fact, who asserts it, who denies it, and where the record leaves it, such as a ruling on it. Where not, state the fact the events agree on.
3. "supporting": the quote that most directly asserts the fact. Copy one item of the quotes list whole: not part of one, and never two joined.
4. "contrary": the quote that most directly denies it, copied the same way; null where the fact is not disputed.

Worked example, from another case, to show the shape. Topic water_safety. The quotes include a city's "The treated water met every federal standard throughout 2015." and a state regulator's "The city's water exceeded the federal action level for lead in the second half of 2015." →
{"disputed": true,
 "summary": "Whether the city's water met federal standards in 2015: the city says it did; the state regulator found it exceeded the lead action level.",
 "supporting": {"quote": "The treated water met every federal standard throughout 2015."},
 "contrary": {"quote": "The city's water exceeded the federal action level for lead in the second half of 2015."}}

queue.reviewer_instructions:
A model read every dated event on this topic and found a fact one side asserts and another denies. You are deciding whether that holds before the dispute is published.

Read both quotes against their pages: each names the stored file and the page it sits on. Keep the dispute where the two quotes state opposite positions on the same fact. Mark it not disputed where they talk past each other, or where a quote is not the position the summary says it is. Correct the summary so it names the fact, who asserts it, who denies it, and where the record leaves it.

The statements, speakers and pin cites beside the quotes are the model's reading of each event on the topic; the quotes are what the pages say.

import html import pathlib import pandas as pd from app.models.spans import Span ATTRIBUTION = ( "Filings from CourtListener's RECAP archive, run by Free Law Project. The events, dates, " "speakers, topics and disputes are a model's reading of them, each pinned to the words it " "quotes; Free Law Project did not produce, endorse or verify this reading." ) def transform(chronology, disputes, output_dir, citation_provider): events = [_list_event(citation_provider, ordinal, row) for ordinal, row in enumerate(chronology.to_dict("records"))] topics = [_list_dispute(citation_provider, ordinal, row) for ordinal, row in enumerate(disputes.to_dict("records"))] path = pathlib.Path(output_dir) / "index.html" path.write_text(_write_page(events, topics), encoding="utf-8") return pd.DataFrame({"path": [str(path)]}) def _link_quote(citation_provider, stage_id, ordinal, column, cell, label): span = Span.model_validate(cell) url = citation_provider.cite_span(stage_id, ordinal, column, span, label=label) return '' + html.escape(span.quote) + "" def _list_event(citation_provider, ordinal, row): quote = _link_quote(citation_provider, "chronology", ordinal, "span", row["span"], row["pin_cite"]) heading = " · ".join(html.escape(str(row[name])) for name in ("date", "speaker", "topic")) return ("

  • " + heading + "

    " + html.escape(row["statement"]) + "

    " "
    " + quote + " (" + html.escape(row["pin_cite"]) + ")
    • ") def _list_dispute(citation_provider, ordinal, row): sides = [] for column in ("supporting", "contrary"): quotes = [_link_quote(citation_provider, "disputes", ordinal, column, cell, row["topic"] + ", " + column) for cell in row[column]] sides.append("

    " + column + ": " + (" / ".join(quotes) or "none found") + "

    ") return ("

  • " + html.escape(row["topic"]) + " · " + html.escape(row["status"]) + "

    " + html.escape(row["summary"]) + "

    " + "".join(sides) + "
    • ") def _write_page(events, topics): return ("US v. Boeing: chronology" "

    United States v. The Boeing Company: chronology

    " "

    " + html.escape(ATTRIBUTION) + "

    " "

    Events

      " + "".join(events) + "
    " "

    Facts one side asserts and another denies

      " + "".join(topics) + "
    ")
